title: High cocaine levels killed Yukon man, inquest told
article: A Whitehorse man who died in a 2008 altercation with police was killed by high levels of cocaine in his body, a coroner's inquest jury was told Thursday.

The week-long inquest is examining the circumstances around the death of Grant McLeod, 39, who went into medical distress while Whitehorse RCMP were trying to arrest him at the Chilkoot Trail Inn on the morning of Aug. 30, 2008.
Officers had been called to the hotel to investigate complaints that McLeod was staggering around with a syringe in his hand.
An autopsy has suggested that McLeod had lethal amounts of cocaine in his system, but the coroner's inquest was called because he died in police custody.
Forensic toxicologist Walter Martz told the six-person inquest panel Thursday that McLeod had 2.3 milligrams of cocaine per litre of blood in his system.
Martz said he's never seen anyone alive with that amount of cocaine in their body.
Later Thursday, forensic pathologist Charles Lee testified that the amount of cocaine in McLeod's body was the underlying factor that led to his death.

Lee said such high levels of coke would explain McLeod's bizarre behaviour and abnormal strength as he struggled with police at the hotel. The amount of cocaine itself would have been enough to kill McLeod, Lee said.
RCMP officers testified Wednesday that they struggled to arrest McLeod, who was very strong and was resisting arrest.
One officer said she employed a choke hold to subdue McLeod, who was ramming her head against a door frame at the same time.

Lee testified there was some indication McLeod had high blood pressure and track marks on his arms, feet and legs. He also identified fractured cartilage in McLeod's neck as well as fibrosis, or scarring, in the heart.
Under questioning, Lee said the officer's choke hold and the struggle to control McLeod may have contributed to his death.
However, Lee testified that the fractured cartilage would not have blocked breathing. As well, McLeod still had a pulse when the ambulance arrived.
As for the fibrosis, Lee said additional stress from a fight or drug use could have killed McLeod at any time.
The jury heard Wednesday afternoon from an ambulance attendant, nurse and emergency room doctor who all tried to revive McLeod.

Ambulance attendant Rob Dawe testified he arrived on the scene to find McLeod laying on the floor, with his eyes fixed and dilated, suggesting a drug overdose or trauma that has put a person near death.
Paramedics began CPR and assisted breathing and did not stop until McLeod was in the emergency room at Whitehorse General Hospital, the jury was told.
Hospital nurse Leatha Smith testified that they continued resuscitation attempts on McLeod over the course of 20 minutes, even employing a drug designed to kick-start the heart.
Smith and Dr. Marc Pronovost testified they could not find any veins into which they could inject an intravenous needle because of all the track marks on McLeod's arms, legs and feet.
Pronovost told the inquest jury he eventually inserted the needle into the femoral artery in McLeod's leg.
Pronovost said there was not much else that could have been done medically even if he had known what drugs McLeod had taken and what kind of struggle McLeod had had with police.
Pronovost declared McLeod dead just after 8 a.m., about an hour after the hotel incident began.
